query_title: Block link-local and localhost service/endpoint addresses in apiserver proxy
query_body:
Reported by @stephenR

It's possible to turn the master into a proxy to localhost or the GCE metadata server by adding a new endpoint that points to the service.

To reproduce, add a new endpoint by posting to http://apiserver/api/v1beta3/endpoints with a description like:

[CODE_BLOCK]

If you then go to http://apiserver/api/v1beta3/proxy/namespaces/default/services/myendpoint/ you can interact with the master's metadata server.

We can't validate that Endpoints are within the cluster CIDR because we deliberately allow importing of external addresses -- that was the original purpose of allowing users to post Endpoints. 

I wouldn't disallow link-local and localhost addresses in Endpoints, either, since that might be useful in the future. I'd prefer to just disallow proxying to such addresses. 

Obviously we'd need to resolve DNS names before checking.

See also #8871

cc @roberthbailey @a-robinson @stephenR @lavalamp
original_body:
The current default behavior of kubectl proxy is to listen on all addresses on port 8001. Thus anyone on the same network gets full access to the apiserver of my cluster.
It would be good to default to listen on localhost and maybe add a flag to override this behavior.

The second issue is that the proxy is vulnerable to dns rebinding. I.e. if I'm running a kubectl proxy and browse the web at the same time, a malicious website can interact with the local apiserver. The recommended way to protect against dns rebinding is to check the Host header for expected values if present.

query_title: Proposal: In-container command execution & port forwarding
query_body:
# In-container command execution & port forwarding

This describes an approach for providing support for:
- executing commands in containers, with stdin/stdout/stderr streams attached
- port forwarding to containers

There are several issues/PRs currently open that are related:
- [Support attach](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1521)
- [Real container ssh](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1513)
- [Provide easy debug network access to services](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1863)
- [OpenShift container command execution proposal](https://github.com/openshift/origin/pull/576)

Note: this approach does not provide SSH support. Instead, it uses SPDY via HTTP, so a custom client is required (i.e. [INLINE_CODE]).
## Flow

Clients should be able to use [INLINE_CODE] to perform remote command execution and port forwarding to containers. [INLINE_CODE] will talk to the API Server and use its proxy support to proxy the execution or port forwarding request to the appropriate kubelet. The proxy connection will be upgraded from HTTP to SPDY, as SPDY supports multiplexing multiple streams across a single connection.
## Proposed changes
### kubectl

Add a new [INLINE_CODE] command that results in the user-specified command being executed in the desired container.

Add a new [INLINE_CODE] command that forwards connections to local ports to remote ports in the desired container.

~~Similar to ssh, it should also be pos
original_body:
Forked from #1503.

We should decide whether we will support [Docker attach to stdin and stdout](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/docker_remote_api_v1.13/#attach-to-a-container). It would be convenient for interactive containers and, more importantly, short-running, run-once data-in/data-out containers, such as for configuration generators, workflow steps, cron jobs, etc.

Support would likely be similar to that required to support run in container (aka docker exec) and/or ssh (#1513).

/cc @vishh

query_title: Go tests share one client causing rate limits to be exceeded
query_body: The Go end to end tests share one client and this often causes the rate limits to be exceeded and the end to end tests to fail (the shell tests have a client per invocation of [INLINE_CODE]). We should change the Go tests to use a fresh client for each test. This would also help to identify individual tests that exceed rate limits. Related to #3667 @bgrant0607 @filbranden @zmerlynn @roberthbailey
original_body:
Kubernetes rate-limits read-only requests and returns 503 when the rate is exceeded:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/3ade280f8981a6954065c63c3f16fe42ab2169d0/pkg/apiserver/handlers.go#L68

Sometimes e2e fails due to rejections, and rejections are a pain for clients. For instance, we wouldn't want kubectl to fail due to this.

The server should add a Retry-After header, and the client should automatically retry such rejections.

query_body:
This is a proposal to implement caching selector result. https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/4817#issuecomment-76495394

AFAIK, currently only [two components](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/labels.md#api) use selector to group their members: [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE], and they get list of their members by matching seletor against all pods' label every time.

Here I propose a way to cache seletor result in etcd.

Define a new registry in etcd: selector.

Whenever a [INLINE_CODE] or [INLINE_CODE] is created, generate [uid](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/identifiers.md#uids) for its selector, and register selector with that uid in etcd. While creating [INLINE_CODE] or [INLINE_CODE], it watches that selector in etcd to wait updates on result of selector. We should add pre-existed matched pods to its result of course.

And whenever a [INLINE_CODE] is created, matches its label with all selector under its namespace (assuming we forbidden selector select object in another ns, which I not quite sure), and add that pod to selector result if match. Update or delete a [INLINE_CODE] should also update all selectors' result under its ns.

When a [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] is created at same time, we should use some kind of mutex to avoid race condition.

Any comment?

query_title: Record pod StartTime when we receive a watch notification on the kubelet
query_body:
Forked from: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/9792#issuecomment-113213791, https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/7868#issuecomment-99706316

Proposal for StartTime modification:
1. Initialize StartTime, once, when the kubelet gets an add notification for the pod
2. If something else modifies it via the apiserver the kubelet will ignore the modification (we can probably evolve this to have the kublet correct any meddling)
3. If the pod is deleted and re-added, the timestamp will change, but not otherwise
4. If the kubelet is slow in dealing with a watch notification (eg: because of pod deletes) the StartTime will include that.

Such a timestamp would be helpful in measuring apiserver -> node watch latencies as well. Node team, thoughts? 

Fyi we can approximate the time it's currently recording as StartTime by sorting the startedAt timestamp of the containers of the pod.

@derekwaynecarr

query_title: Better memory manager at node to guarantee QoS
query_body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14452...

We introduced QoS concept and API to Kubernetes 1.1 release, but lack of the support on node side to ensure QoS. Filed this umbrella issue for memory management for current known issues:
1. At node level, the only improvement was introduced is OOM score based on the resource class. This means we fully rely on Kernel sys OOM to react. This is dangerous, which could put the node to totally unstable mode. Based on my experience dealing with internal system, when sys OOM is triggered, before kernel kills some processes, process kswapd might use 100% CPU on a node to reclaim some pages, which could include disk io too, thus. All user processes are significantly slow down. **You can overcommit on request or limit, but Kernel sys OOM should be prevented**
2. This also means we should introduce a userspace memory manager to detect system overcommit on memory at run time. When memory pressure on the node is pretty high, and kubelet should proactively kill some lower priority containers / pods. We don't have this for today. 
3. Docker doesn't do process tracking at all except root pid. This means if sys OOM kills a non-root process in a container, container itself would be still running. 
4. Without userspace OOM handling support, even kernel kills container's root process, Kubelet might restart one to maintain sys OOM situation. 
5. Today all containers are at root level, instead of using cgroup_parent based on QoS.
